q: It is your first morning on the charter yacht. What do you check before you start the engine?
a: Oil, coolant, belt and the raw-water strainer
o: Fuel gauge only — the base checks the rest
Battery water and the spark plug leads
Gearbox oil and the shaft anode only
why: Daily check: oil and coolant levels, belt tension, strainer clear, bilge dry, fuel on.

q: At the fuel quay the attendant reaches for the nozzle marked 'Unleaded 95'. What do you do?
a: Stop him — the engine takes diesel only
o: Let him — any fuel will do for one fill
Let him, then add a bottle of additive
Let him if the tank is half full of diesel
why: Yacht engines are diesels; petrol in the tank means draining it, with a fire risk and engine damage.

q: You have just started the engine. What do you check at the stern before casting off?
a: Cooling water spurting out with the exhaust
o: Black smoke coming out with the exhaust
Bubbles rising from the propeller
A thin film of oil on the water astern
why: No water from the exhaust means no cooling flow: stop the engine and check the seacock and strainer.

q: You are settling in for the evening at anchor. Which battery do you run the boat from?
a: The house battery, keeping the engine one for starting
o: The engine battery, saving the house one for the night
Both together, so they share the load evenly
Whichever one shows the higher voltage
why: Domestic loads run from the house bank; the engine battery stays isolated so you can always start.

lines: Evening at anchor
Fridge, lights and music to run

q: You are motoring in open water, well clear of other boats, when this happens. What do you do?
a: Stop the engine, then check the cooling water intake
o: Raise the revs to pump more water through
Carry on — the harbour is only 2 miles away
Open the coolant cap at once to top it up
why: Overheating with little exhaust water means the raw-water flow has failed: stop before the engine is damaged.

lines: Alarm sounding
Exhaust: steam, very little water

q: This alarm goes off as you motor across the bay. What do you do?
a: Stop the engine at once and check the oil level
o: Carry on at low revs to the next harbour
Top up the coolant, then carry on
Ignore it — the temperature is normal
why: Low oil pressure can wreck a diesel within minutes; stop it and find out why.

lines: Oil pressure alarm and warning light

q: You are going to clean the strainer. What is the right order?
a: Close the seacock, clean the strainer, open the seacock
o: Open the strainer lid with the seacock left open
Clean it with the engine running to flush it
Clean it, then leave the seacock shut to be safe
why: Close the seacock first or the sea pours in; reopen it before starting or the engine overheats again.

fig.title: Raw-water strainer
lines: Engine stopped after overheating
Strainer bowl packed with sea grass
Seacock open

q: How much fuel will be left when you arrive?
a: 30 litres — well above the reserve
o: 20 litres — just above the reserve
10 litres — below the reserve
45 litres — well above the reserve
why: 30 M ÷ 6 kn = 5 h; 5 h × 4 L/h = 20 L used; 50 − 20 = 30 L left.

lines: Today's leg: 30 M under engine, calm
Keep at least 15 L in reserve

q: What do you do about the house battery?
a: Run the engine to charge it, or plug in to shore power
o: Switch to BOTH and leave it there overnight
Nothing — 11.9 V means it is fully charged
Switch off the engine battery to save power
why: 11.9 V at rest is a well-flattened house bank; recharge it from the alternator or shore power.

lines: Second night at anchor, fridge on
Cabin lights dim

q: You arrive in a marina and want shore power. In what order do you connect the cable?
a: Boat end first, then the shore pillar
o: Shore pillar first, then the boat end
Either way — the cable is waterproof
Both ends at once, with the breaker on
why: Plug in at the boat first so there is never a live loose end; unplug at the pillar first.

q: Your crew is in the shower when this happens. What is wrong?
a: Tank 1 is empty — switch off the pump, change tanks
o: The pump fuse has blown — replace it
The water heater has an air lock — run the engine
The shower drain is blocked — clear it
why: A pump that runs on while the taps spit air has emptied its tank; a pump running dry can burn out.

fig.title: Fresh water
lines: Pump runs and does not stop
Taps spit air, then nothing
Two tanks, selector set to tank 1

q: You are moored stern-to in a busy town harbour. Where should the heads empty to?
a: Into the holding tank, to be emptied well offshore
o: Straight overboard — the harbour flushes it out
Into the bilge — the bilge pump clears it later
Into the grey-water drain under the galley
why: In harbours and anchorages the heads go to the holding tank; empty it well out at sea or at a pump-out.

q: Your crew has finished cooking pasta. How do they turn off the gas?
a: Solenoid off, let the flame die, then the burner knob
o: Burner knob off first, then the solenoid
Burner knob only — the solenoid stays on all week
Bottle valve only, the next morning
why: Shutting the supply first lets the flame burn off the gas left in the pipe, so none sits in the line.

q: You come below and smell gas in the saloon. What do you do?
a: Turn off the bottle, no switches or flames, air the boat
o: Turn on the cabin fan to blow the gas out
Run the electric bilge pump to clear it
Light the stove to burn off what is left
why: Gas is heavier than air and any spark can ignite it: shut the supply, leave the switches alone, ventilate.

q: The bilge is fuller than usual. The electric bilge pump is on AUTO but stays silent. What do you do?
a: Pump by hand, then check the fuse and float switch
o: Wait — on AUTO it will start by itself
Run the engine — it pumps the bilge as it cools
Turn the battery switch off and on again
why: Use the manual pump to keep up, then look for a blown fuse or a jammed float switch.

q: The engine note changes suddenly as you motor along. What has most likely happened?
a: A rope has wrapped round the propeller
o: Air has got into the fuel system
The raw-water intake has blocked
The gearbox has slipped into neutral
why: A thump, vibration and lost speed near floats point to a rope round the prop: neutral, and stop the engine.

fig.title: Motoring past fishing floats
lines: A thump under the stern
Heavy vibration, the engine labours
Speed drops, though the revs are the same

q: The engine is running, yet the battery is not charging. What is the likely cause?
a: The alternator belt is slack or broken
o: The house battery is fully charged
The fuel filter is partly blocked
The shore power cable is still plugged in
why: No charge plus a squealing belt means a slipping belt; on many engines it also drives the water pump.

lines: Engine running, charge warning light on
A squeal from the engine box at start-up

q: You turn the key to leave the anchorage. Why will the engine not start?
a: On BOTH the fridge drained the engine battery too
o: The house battery is fine, so the starter has failed
Overnight the fuel has drained back to the tank
The engine battery charges only from shore power
why: BOTH joins the banks, so domestic loads flatten the starting battery as well; keep it isolated.

fig.title: Morning at anchor
lines: Battery switch left on BOTH all night
Fridge and lights ran from 18:00
Starter clicks but will not turn the engine

q: The overheat alarm goes off close to this rocky shore. What do you do first?
a: Unroll the genoa and sail clear, then stop the engine
o: Stop the engine at once and drift while you check it
Keep motoring flat out to get clear quickly
Go below and clear the strainer with it running
why: The boat's safety first: get sea room under sail, then stop the engine before it is damaged.

lines: Overheat alarm, little exhaust water
Rocky shore 0.3 M downwind, F4 onshore

q: You have cleared the strainer, but the problem remains. What do you suspect, and what do you do?
a: A failed impeller — stop and call the lead crew
o: An empty fuel tank — refill and restart
A full holding tank — pump it out at sea
A flat battery — switch to BOTH and restart
why: With the intake clear, no flow points to the raw-water pump impeller; the lead crew's engineer can change it.

fig.title: After clearing the strainer
lines: Seacock open, strainer clean
Engine restarted: still no water at the exhaust
Lead boat 3 M away, calm sea
